llm.answer: This is my best recollection, not a verified citation, and the docket number is a guess. The proposed AD covers Bombardier Challenger 300 (BD-100-1A10) airplanes. The unsafe condition is blockage of the cabin pressure safety valve sensing port by RTV silicone, foam, or insulation debris, which can cause loss of cabin pressurization. The proposal would require a one-time detailed inspection of the sensing port and associated lines for debris. It would also require removing any debris found and corrective action as needed, following the Bombardier service information. The AD would apply to BD-100-1A10 airplanes within the listed serial number range.

Yes, as best I recall, the FAA has proposed an AD (NPRM) for Columbia Helicopters Model 234 and restricted category CH-47D helicopters. It would require repetitive borescope inspections of the flight control rigid connecting links for corrosion, and replacement of any link found corroded. The docket number I cite is from memory and may be wrong, so please check it against the Federal Register before relying on it.

I am answering from memory and cannot confirm the FR or docket number or the exact thresholds. The proposed AD would apply to EC135 and EC635 helicopters with the affected yaw actuator and control rod installed. It would require a one-time inspection of the ball pivot (for play, wear, damage or cracks), the control rod, and the yaw actuator. It would also require repetitive ball pivot checks at a set interval in flight hours. Parts that fail the inspections would have to be replaced before further flight. Operators would have to report the inspection results to Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH within a stated time after each inspection. Compliance would follow the Airbus Helicopters Alert Service Bulletin for the EC135 and EC635, as mandated by the corresponding EASA AD.

Yes, as best I recall. The FAA proposed an AD for Airbus Helicopters Deutschland EC135 and MBB-BK 117 C-2/D-2 helicopters that requires repetitive inspections for cracks in the rescue hoist cable drum. It would also require corrective action, such as replacing the drum, if cracks are found. This is from memory, and I am not confident in the docket number cited, so verify it before relying on it.

Yes, as best I recall, the FAA withdrew this NPRM. It proposed inspecting power feeder cables, troughs and caterpillar grommets on McDonnell Douglas DC-9 and MD-81/-82 airplanes. I cannot confirm the withdrawal notice's FR document number, and the docket number cited is a low-confidence guess.

Yes. As I recall, the FAA proposed an AD (NPRM) for certain Boeing 787-8 airplanes. It would require inspecting the large forward cargo door split frames, which may have been made from nonconforming material, to check for the nonconforming condition. Corrective action would follow if the condition is found. I am working from memory, so the docket number I cited is my best guess and should be checked against the Federal Register.

Yes. As I recall, the FAA withdrew this NPRM, which would have required shield assemblies on the power feeder cables in the forward and aft lower cargo compartments of MD-80 series airplanes. I am answering from memory, and the docket number and the withdrawal notice are not verified, so treat the citation as a best guess.

Yes. I recall an FAA NPRM covering Boeing 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 airplanes. It addresses reports that VHF radio active and standby frequencies swapped without flightcrew input. The cause is tuning control panel (TCP) software. The proposed AD would require installing updated TCP software, and possibly a related software or configuration check. I am working from memory and am not sure of the docket number, so please verify it against the Federal Register.

Yes, as best I recall, the FAA proposed an AD for Boeing 787-8, -9 and -10 airplanes. It would shorten the compliance times for a detailed inspection of the vertical fin tension bolt holes for corrosion and a check of the bolt sealant, with corrective actions if findings are discovered. I am working from memory and am not certain of the docket number cited, so please verify it against the Federal Register.

Yes, I believe there is an NPRM for Piper PA-34-200 (Seneca) airplanes. It would require a life limit on the alternate (non-original part number) bolts that attach the nose landing gear drag link. Operators would have to replace the bolts at the life limit and could not install them past that limit. The cited docket number is my best recollection and I could not verify it, so check the exact docket and FR document number and the compliance times against the Federal Register.

Yes, as best I recall, the FAA proposed an AD for CFM International CFM56-5B, -5C and -7B turbofan engines. It addresses separation of the honeycomb on the HPT stage 1 inner stationary seal, which can cause loss of seal function and damage to the engine. The proposal would require repetitive borescope inspections of the seal, and replacement of the seal if the honeycomb has separated or inspection limits are exceeded. I am not certain of the docket number or the Federal Register document number, so the citation above is a best guess and should be checked.

I believe an FAA NPRM does cover this. It would apply to Boeing 737-600/-700/-800/-900ER airplanes and address a thrust reverser upper locking hydraulic actuator whose proximity sensor target is out of adjustment. A misadjusted target could falsely indicate the reverser is locked, which could allow an in-flight deployment. The proposed action is an inspection or adjustment of the sensor target, plus corrective actions as needed, per a Boeing service bulletin. I am working from memory and am not sure of the docket number, so please verify FAA-2023-1403 against the Federal Register before relying on it.

Being an A350-941 is necessary but not enough. These proposed ADs usually cover only A350-941 airplanes (and sometimes -1041) that have an affected HMU installed, or that could have one installed, as identified in the referenced EASA AD. I can't confirm the docket or FR document number from memory, so check it against the NPRM itself. Applicability depends on the HMU part numbers and serial numbers fitted to your engines, and possibly on the airplane MSN. Until you check those against the EASA AD and the NPRM's applicability paragraph, I can't say it applies. Look up the installed HMU P/N and S/N on each Trent XWB engine, then compare them with the affected list in the EASA AD. If an affected HMU is installed, the replacement before the reduced life limit would apply. Otherwise the airplane is likely not affected, but you would need to keep the AD's prohibition on installing affected HMUs in mind.

Likely yes. This is from memory and I could not verify the document or docket number, so treat the cited docket as a best guess. The proposed AD covers Bombardier CL-600-2B16 airplanes (Challenger 601-3A, 601-3R, 604 and similar variants) in the transport category. It would require revising the AFM with procedures for an uncommanded, unarrested flap movement accompanied by a FLAPS FAIL caution message. A 601-3R is within the CL-600-2B16 type certificate, so it should be covered, subject to confirming your serial number against the applicability paragraph of the NPRM.

Likely yes. As I recall, the proposed AD covers Airbus Helicopters Deutschland EC135 series helicopters, including the P2+, with a sliding door emergency exit installed. It would require installing additional placards or labels with opening instructions. The docket number I cite is a best guess from memory, so please verify it. Applicability depends on your helicopter actually having the sliding door installed. Check the applicability paragraph and the referenced service information in the NPRM to confirm.

Most likely not. The proposed AD covers Dauphin-family models (such as the SA-365, AS365 and EC155 series) and their main rotor servo-controls. The AS350B3 belongs to the Ecureuil/AStar family, which is not in that applicability list. I cannot recall the exact FR document or docket number, so I have not cited one. Check the applicability paragraph of the NPRM to confirm that the AS350B3 is not listed.

Most likely not. This is from memory and I could not verify it. The proposed AD would supersede the earlier wing root rib AD for the ASW-15 and add the ASW-15B. Its applicability is limited to those two models, so an ASW-20 (utility category) is not listed. The utility category does not change that. The docket number I cited is a best guess, not a confirmed match. Check the applicability paragraph of the actual NPRM and your glider's model and serial number. If an ASW-20 is ever named in the final AD, the answer would change.

Probably yes. The PW4060 is a PW4000 94-inch fan series engine, and I recall the Pb sensor replacement proposal covering that family. The reported failures (tailpipe fire, loss of thrust control, in-flight shutdowns from undetected sensor deterioration) match what I remember of that proposal. I could not confirm the exact document number or the affected part numbers and serial numbers from memory. The docket number above is a best guess, so please check it. Then check whether your engines have an affected Pb sensor installed, since applicability usually depends on the sensor part number.

Probably yes. From memory, the proposed AD covers Hélicoptères Guimbal Cabri G2 helicopters of all serial numbers, certificated in the normal category, and it is not limited to a serial-number range. Since your Cabri G2 is normal category, you can expect it to apply whatever your serial number is. I can't recall the exact FR document or docket number, so I haven't cited one. Check the applicability paragraph in the NPRM itself. If it limits applicability to helicopters with a particular ELT or antenna installation, confirm that against your helicopter's configuration.

To the best of my recollection, this NPRM (Rolls-Royce plc RB211-535 series engines with radial drive steady bearing P/N LK76084, docket 2003-NE-31-AD) was withdrawn by the FAA and is no longer active. A withdrawn NPRM imposes no requirements, so no AD obligation arises from it. I cannot give the Federal Register document number of the withdrawal notice from memory, and my recollection of the withdrawal itself is not certain, so please confirm on the Federal Register or regulations.gov docket.

From memory, and with low confidence, the NPRM under docket FAA-2010-0720 (Sikorsky S-92A, reduced main gearbox housing life limit) is no longer active. I believe the FAA withdrew it after the life-limit issue was handled through revisions to the Airworthiness Limitations Section instead of an AD. I cannot recall the withdrawal's Federal Register document number or its date, so please check the docket on regulations.gov or the Federal Register for the final status.

From memory, and without confirmation: the NPRM under docket FAA-2010-0427 would have superseded AD 2002-20-01 for Bell HH-1K/TH-1F/TH-1L/UH-1 series and Southwest Florida Aviation SW204/SW205 helicopters. I believe the FAA later withdrew it, so the comment period is closed and the proposal is not open. AD 2002-20-01 stays in effect. I cannot give the withdrawal notice's Federal Register document number, so please check the docket on regulations.gov to confirm.

From memory, and with limited confidence, this proposal is no longer active. I believe the FAA withdrew the NPRM for Bombardier DHC-8-400 series airplanes (fuel coupling and bonding wire wear) under docket FAA-2018-0547. A withdrawal does not prohibit the FAA from issuing a later, similar proposal. I cannot recall the Federal Register document numbers for the NPRM or the withdrawal notice, so please check the docket on regulations.gov to confirm.

From memory, and without documents to check, I believe this proposed AD (Boeing 737-600/-700/-800/-900 thrust reverser hydraulic actuator rod end and attach fitting inspections) is no longer open. I think the FAA withdrew the NPRM and did not issue a final rule under docket FAA-2011-0254. I cannot give the Federal Register document number of the withdrawal notice. The withdrawal is the best-supported status, but it should be confirmed on regulations.gov or in the Federal Register.

From memory, and not verified against the Federal Register, the July 2013 NPRM under docket FAA-2013-0627 is no longer active. I believe the FAA withdrew it rather than issuing a final rule. An NPRM is only a proposal, so the existing AD on BAe 146 and Avro 146-RJ main landing gear life limits would stay in force unless a later final rule supersedes it. I cannot give the withdrawal notice's document number with confidence, so please check the docket on regulations.gov.
(no parsable answer)

I could not identify the NPRM's FR document or docket number, so this is a best-effort answer from general knowledge, not a verified reading of the bulletin. Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1358 RB (Nov. 17, 2025) is a wing-structure (ATA 57) bulletin for 737-8, -9 and -8200 airplanes. The proposed AD would most likely require an inspection of the identified wing structure, such as a detailed or eddy-current inspection, within a compliance time set by the bulletin's grouping. That time is probably counted from the airplane's total flight cycles or flight hours or from the AD effective date. If the inspection finds cracking, damage or a nonconforming condition, the operator would have to repair it before further flight, or by a set time, using the bulletin's procedures or an FAA-approved method. The operator would also have to report findings to Boeing where the bulletin requires it. Airplanes outside the bulletin's effectivity are not affected. The exact thresholds, repeat intervals and repair steps are in the bulletin and the NPRM's compliance paragraphs, and I have not verified them.

I cannot confirm from memory that a final rule has been issued. The question does not identify which NPRM it means. Several Boeing 737-800 (737NG) structural cracking actions exist, and I cannot match this one to a specific docket or FR document number without guessing. If the NPRM has been finalized, the final rule would be published in the Federal Register as an AD under 14 CFR 39.13. It would take effect on the stated effective date, usually about 35 days after publication, and stay in force until superseded, revised or terminated. To check, search the FAA Dynamic Regulatory System or Federal Register.gov for the NPRM's docket number and look for a later 'Final rule' entry. I will not cite a document number I cannot verify.

The question has a mismatch: the A320-214 is an Airbus model, not a Boeing one. I cannot identify a specific NPRM that matches it, and I will not invent a document number, inspection requirement, or compliance time. Airbus A320-series ADs usually require a detailed or eddy-current inspection of the affected structure, with repair if cracking is found. Compliance times are normally set in flight cycles or flight hours from a stated threshold, or within a fixed number of months. The actual requirement and compliance time depend on the specific NPRM and the service information it cites. Please provide the FR document number or docket number, or confirm the manufacturer and model, so I can answer precisely.

I can't identify which NPRM this is, so this is a best estimate. Rotorcraft flight manual revision NPRMs typically estimate about 1 work-hour at $85 per hour, which is $85 per helicopter in labor. On that basis the total would be about $4,250 for an assumed 50 U.S.-registered helicopters. The $85 figure is the more reliable part; the total depends on the actual fleet count in the NPRM.

I can't identify the specific 1996 AD with confidence, and I have no documents to check. My best recollection is that the 737 lap-joint cracking requirements descend from AD 93-07-15 and the related Boeing service bulletin program. That program required an initial inspection of the fuselage lap joints once the airplane reached a flight-cycle threshold or within a set time after the AD's effective date. Repeat inspections followed at fixed flight-cycle intervals, on the order of a few thousand cycles. Any cracking found had to be repaired, and some actions required terminating modifications. The exact thresholds and intervals are not something I can state reliably; check the AD text and the service bulletin it cites.
